newsitem.title: UK: U.S. study finds out why tumours so hard to kill.
newsitem.headline: U.S. study finds out why tumours so hard to kill.

text.p: American researchers said on Thursday they had found a new reason why cancer can be so hard to kill.

Not only do individual genes mutate and cause cells to divide out of control -- a well-established fact. The chromosomes on which genes live can also become unstable and change form, they reported in the science journal Nature.

"What we found is that there exists another form of instability which has nothing to do with mutations. It is an instability of the chromosomes themselves," said Christov Lengauer of the Johns Hopkins Oncology Centre in Baltimore, who worked on the study.
Lengauer said the instability showed up right at the beginning of tumour formation, which indicated it was a cause, rather than an effect, of the cancer.
The group worked with colo-rectal cancers but said it was likely the findings would translate to other forms of cancer.
Lengauer said cancer research had long ago established the tendency of cells to mutate. Normally the body can control the little bits of damage that build up and cause mutations.
But sometimes genes known as "mismatch and repair" genes themselves become defective.

"When those genes are defective, they work as a kind of accelerator because they allow the mutations to stay in the genome (all the body's genes)," Lengauer, a molecular biologist, said in a telephone interview.
This mismatch and repair defect could be found in about 15 percent of colon cancers, he said. The question was -- what was causing the other 85 percent?
Lengauer said he believed this new chromosomal instability mechanism could be responsible.
"We say it is two pathways of instability," he said. "You have two groups of cancer -- one with the defect in mismatch and repair and the other group is one that has chromosomal instability."

Lengauer said there were no immediate implications for treating cancer. But he said one of the biggest problems in treating cancer was that the tumour cells all varied slightly, a condition known as tumour heterogeneity.

"There are a lot of different cells in the tumour and they all behave a little bit differently," he said. "That means some cells escape treatment such as chemotherapy." He added: "This chromosomal instability might be the driving force behind this heterogeneity. What we will try to do now is try to understand the biochemical mechanism for this."
There could even be a genetic cause for the chromosomal instability, he said.
